title: Projected altermagnetism by symmetry reduction at surfaces and in thin films
authors: Sopheak Sorn, Charanpreet Singh, Lukasz Plucinski, Gustav Bihlmayer, Yuriy Mokrousov, Wulf Wulfhekel
abstract: Altermagnets are a newly identified class of magnetic materials that combine vanishing net magnetization within the unit cell with spin-split electronic states. Their theoretical description relies on symmetry properties of the bulk band structure. Surfaces and thin films, however, inherently break these symmetries. Here, we investigate the consequences of such symmetry reduction for the electronic structure of bulk altermagnets near the surface and of thin films. When the surface coincides with a symmetry plane of the bulk altermagnetic order, the resulting two-dimensional Brillouin zone exhibits spin-degenerate bands, corresponding to conventional antiferromagnetic behavior. In all other cases, the symmetry of the altermagnetic order is reduced, leading to modified spin splitting. Remarkably, we discover a thin-film geometry of a $g$-wave altermagnet with a particular surface orientation that enables a $d$-wave spin splitting, which is commonly accompanied by the spin-splitter effect, suggesting the functionalization of non-$d$-wave altermagnets by surfaces. Our findings demonstrate that symmetry breaking at surfaces and in thin films fundamentally reshapes altermagnetic spin textures, providing a tunable platform for controlling spin-dependent electronic phenomena.
summary: This work explores how cutting a bulk altermagnetic material into thin films or exposing its surfaces fundamentally changes its magnetic electronic structure. By applying group theory and advanced calculations, the authors show that surface orientation dictates whether the spin splitting is conventional, ferromagnetic-like, or possesses a desirable d-wave symmetry. This demonstrates that surface engineering offers a powerful route to tune quantum magnetic properties.
main_problem: The study investigates how breaking crystal symmetries at surfaces and in thin films fundamentally alters the electronic structure and spin-splitting patterns of bulk altermagnetic materials.
main_result: Symmetry reduction dictates that while some surfaces yield conventional antiferromagnetic behavior, specific orientations (like (210)) can stabilize desirable d-wave spin splitting, suggesting surface engineering is a tunable platform for controlling magnetism.
method: The research combines group-theoretical analysis of symmetry constraints with first-principles electronic structure calculations (DFT/Tight-Binding) to model the projected band structures.
model_or_system: The system under study is altermagnetic materials, exemplified by CrSb. The theoretical framework analyzes the spin splitting term in the Bloch Hamiltonian based on the material's magnetic octupole moment and the symmetry of the terminating surface plane.
key_observables: Spin-split electronic states (momentum-dependent), the symmetry of the spin splitting (e.g., d-wave vs. ferromagnetic-like), and the presence/absence of spin degeneracy in the 2D Brillouin zone.
important_parameters: Surface orientation ((001), (010), (210)), Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) strength, and the nature of the altermagnetic order parameter ($\varphi$).
main_assumptions: Initial analyses rely on a bulk-projection picture; some calculations assume fixed atomic positions without structural relaxation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures projected onto surface BZs for different orientations, showing spin degeneracy or specific symmetry splittings (e.g., d-wave splitting confirmed for the (210) plane).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical dependence on symmetry reduction, then analyzing multiple surfaces ((001), (010), (210)) using group theory and DFT/TB calculations to map out how surface termination dictates the resulting spin texture.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of controlling electronic properties via boundary conditions (surfaces) by exploiting symmetry breaking is highly relevant to designing quantum materials for spintronics and topological phenomena.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Illustration of bulk states projecting onto surface BZ in g-wave AM CrSb. (a) Schematic representation of the bulk states at the Fermi level and their Sz spin polar- ization (blue/red) projecting onto the (001) surface BZ (top- most green hexagon) along the direction of the orange line. Blue and red bulk states project onto the same points, lead- ing to spin-degenerate states throughout the surface BZ. (b) Projections of bulk states as computed from DFT onto three surfaces indicate a rich variety of outcomes. ΓA and ΓM pro- jections yield spin-degenerate outcomes (colorless), while ΓK projection strikingly leads to a d-wave spin splitting.

FIG. 2. Crystal structure (a,d,g) of CrSb thin slabs of (001), (010), and (210) orientation, respectively. (b, e, h) display the color-coded z-spin polarization of the projected bulk states at the Fermi level onto the BZ of the slabs highlighting its absence for the (001) and (010) orientation, and its d-wave symmetry for the (210) orientation. To single out surface states, we contrast them with results from the slab calculations shown in (c, f, j), through which the surface states are clearly seen as the additional lines on top of the bulk states.
